A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SceneStaging work and have readable text, equations, figures, and tables. v3 preserves the main paper and adds Appendices A–E. The externally linked videos are not embedded; their written descriptions can be compared, but their visual quality cannot be verified from these PDFs.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations on 2,125 scene–prompt pairs, a 50-participant user study, component ablations, and generated examples.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds quantitative metric–human agreement results and further qualitative analyses.

M1.justification: The SceneStaging architecture, data pipeline, attention loss, and training objective are unchanged. Appendix E adds a downstream application procedure that combines generated keyframes and original scenes with Kling image-to-video synthesis, a limited extension beyond the existing still-image storyboarding pipeline.

E1.justification: Training datasets, the 425-image benchmark, and the DL3DV-10K ablation remain unchanged. Appendix E newly reports two video-synthesis demonstrations using different arrangements of original and generated keyframes, extending coverage to temporal scene preservation. The additional still-image examples do not establish new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The image-generation comparators remain Qwen-Image-Edit, FLUX.1 Kontext Dev, and SceneDecorator. Appendix A adds actual evaluation-method comparisons: CLIP-T against G2.5F-TIA and DreamSim against G2.5F-SA, with scores and human-agreement results rather than the brief metric criticism in v2.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds a metric-validation protocol measuring agreement with human preferences on pairs having clear preferences. The main benchmark, training budget, and generation settings are unchanged. Appendix B's prompts and annotation instructions document the existing evaluation rather than establish that it was redesigned or rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix A supplies substantial evaluation-validity analysis through spatial/action failure cases, scene-similarity counterexamples, and quantitative agreement with human judgments. Appendix C adds visual error analysis of DL3DV-10K composites, including incorrect scale, floating objects, and intersections. v2 only briefly discussed these issues; its original component ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Appendix B.2 newly specifies the human-preference aggregation procedure: majority-agreement filtering followed by contributions weighted as w=1/k^0.8 and normalization. This expands reporting of the existing estimator, without establishing a procedural change. Participant and annotator counts are unchanged; no confidence intervals, repeated-run uncertainty, or formal significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Table 4 adds a new family of evaluator-validation results: human agreement is 83.36% for G2.5F-TIA versus 41.64% for CLIP-T, and 95.63% for G2.5F-SA versus 90.85% for DreamSim. Figures 6–9 add scored metric examples, compositing failures, and qualitative comparisons. All original numerical results in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The method's definitions and Equations 1–11 are unchanged, and no theorem, proof, assumption, or derivation is added. The appendix describes ordinary agreement accuracy and specifies the previously mentioned vote-normalization calculation; it does not introduce new theoretical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, and conclusion are unchanged. Claims concerning the data-construction pipeline, correspondence-guided attention loss, and superior scene/text alignment retain the same scope.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds substantive explanations of CLIP-T's spatial/action insensitivity and DreamSim's sensitivity to foreground changes, zoom, and blur. Appendix E extends the applicability discussion to video keyframe generation. The main interpretation of the ablations and the limitation concerning foreground identity preservation remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Table 5 provides the exact Gemini evaluation prompts. Appendix B documents candidate randomization, select-all annotation instructions, majority filtering, and the previously unspecified normalization parameter and formula. These substantially improve evaluation reproducibility. Appendix E also identifies Kling, keyframe arrangements, and a supplementary-video access link; training implementation details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The same 31 references and main related-work section are retained. Appendix A expands substantive positioning against CLIP-T and DreamSim, including DreamSim's use by SceneDecorator and why these metrics are considered less suitable for the task.

P1.justification: v3 appends five organized supplementary sections and moves the references after them. The main paper's prose, terminology, section order, and narrative are unchanged apart from the version stamp, so this is a structural extension rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with metric-comparison panels in Figures 6–7, compositing examples in Figure 8, an additional baseline-comparison grid in Figure 9, and Tables 4–5 for metric agreement and evaluation prompts. Existing Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–3 retain their content and layout.

improvement.justification: v3 provides a clearer basis for trusting and reproducing the evaluation: metric selection gains direct human-agreement evidence, and previously underspecified scoring and voting procedures become explicit. These strengthen the already reported experiments without changing their results. The gain remains bounded because the new agreement analysis omits valid-pair counts and uncertainty estimates, while the video demonstrations cannot be inspected within the supplied PDFs.
